question: What is a JWT token and what are its three parts?
title: JWT Token Structure — Header, Payload, Signature Explained
direct_answer: A JWT (JSON Web Token) is a compact, URL-safe token format for transmitting claims between parties. It consists of three base64url-encoded parts separated by dots: Header (algorithm and token type), Payload (claims containing user data and metadata), and Signature (cryptographic hash verifying integrity).

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of JWT structure and purpose — foundational knowledge for implementing any JWT-based authentication system
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing base64 encoding with encryption — the payload is readable by anyone, so sensitive data like passwords should never be stored in it
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that the signature prevents tampering but doesn't hide data, and mention that you can decode JWT payloads at jwt.io to inspect claims

sections.title: Understanding JWT Structure and Purpose
sections.content:
JWT (JSON Web Token) is a self-contained authentication token that carries user information in a standardized format.

Think of it like a **digitally signed ID card** — anyone can read the information on it, but they can't forge or alter it without invalidating the signature. The three parts work together: the **header** declares which signing algorithm is used (like HS256 or RS256), the **payload** contains the actual data (user ID, roles, expiration time), and the **signature** is a cryptographic hash that proves the token hasn't been tampered with. Each part is base64url-encoded (NOT encrypted) and joined with dots to form a single string like eyJhbGc.eyJzdWI.TJVA95.

The key insight: JWT enables **stateless authentication** — the server doesn't need to store session data because all necessary information travels with the token, and the signature ensures trust without database lookups.

sections.title: The Three Parts of a JWT
sections.content:
blue|Header|~xxxxx.|JSON naming the algorithm (HS256)|Declares the token type (JWT)|Base64url-encoded, not secret
emerald|Payload|~yyyyy.|Holds the claims (sub, exp, roles)|Readable by anyone — only encoded|Never put passwords or secrets here
violet|Signature|~zzzzz|HMAC/RSA hash of header + payload|Computed with the secret key|Proves the token was not tampered with

sections.title: Creating and Parsing a JWT in Spring Boot
When to Use JWT Tokens
sections.content: Use JWT for **stateless REST APIs** where you need horizontal scaling — multiple server instances can validate tokens without sharing session storage. Perfect for **mobile apps** where the client makes frequent API calls and you want to avoid session cookie complexities. Ideal for **microservices authentication** where a gateway service issues tokens and downstream services independently verify them using the same secret key or public key. Also use JWT for **cross-domain authentication** in single sign-on (SSO) scenarios where one login grants access to multiple related services, because tokens travel easily in HTTP headers unlike cookies with domain restrictions.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Storing passwords in the payload**: Freshers see base64 encoding and think it's secure, but anyone can decode the token at jwt.io and read the payload — only store non-sensitive data like user ID and roles.
- **Using tokens without expiration**: Setting no exp claim means the token is valid forever, so if it's stolen, the attacker has permanent access until you change the secret key globally.
- **Treating the token as encrypted**: The signature only proves integrity (not tampered), not confidentiality (not readable) — if you need to hide data, encrypt the entire token separately or don't put sensitive data in it at all.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Three parts**: Header (algorithm metadata), Payload (claims/data), Signature (tamper-proof hash) — all base64url-encoded and dot-separated
**Base64 vs encryption**: Base64 is encoding for transport, not security — anyone can decode the payload, so never store passwords or API keys
**Signature validation**: The server uses the secret key to verify the token hasn't been modified — any change to header or payload invalidates the signature
**Stateless authentication**: Server doesn't need to query a database or session store to validate the token — all info is self-contained
**Compact format**: URL-safe string that fits in HTTP headers (Authorization: Bearer token) without special encoding
**Token lifetime**: Always include exp claim — tokens should expire (commonly 15 minutes to 24 hours) to limit damage if stolen
**Algorithm choice**: HS256 (symmetric HMAC) for simple apps, RS256 (asymmetric RSA) when issuer and validator are different services

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A JWT token is a self-contained authentication credential that lets servers verify users without storing session data. It's made of three parts joined by dots. The first part is the header, which specifies the signing algorithm like HS256. The second part is the payload, containing claims like the user ID and expiration time. The third part is the signature, which is a cryptographic hash that proves no one tampered with the token. Here's the key thing freshers miss: the payload is base64-encoded, not encrypted. Anyone can paste the token into jwt.io and read the claims. That's why you never put passwords in it. The signature is what makes it secure — you need the secret key to create a valid signature, so even though anyone can read the token, only the server can issue legitimate ones. When a client sends a request, the server extracts the token from the Authorization header, validates the signature using the secret key, checks the expiration, and if everything's valid, the user is authenticated. This enables stateless APIs where you can scale horizontally without sharing session storage across servers. One mistake I'd avoid is forgetting the expiration claim. Without it, stolen tokens work forever until you rotate the global secret key, which breaks all existing tokens for every user.

The payload contains the claims, which is user data like a user ID, roles, and an expiration time. The signature is a cryptographic hash of the header and payload, computed using your server's secret key.

The signature is what makes a JWT trustworthy. When your server receives a token, it recomputes the signature using its secret key. If it matches, the token is valid and hasn't been tampered with. If someone changes a single character in the payload, the signature won't match and the token is rejected.

sharp edge: JWT payload is base64url encoded, not encrypted. Anyone who intercepts a JWT can decode the payload and read everything in it. This is a common misconception — encoding and encryption are completely different things. Never put passwords, credit card numbers, or any sensitive data in a JWT payload.

question: What are JWT claims and what standard claims should you include?
title: JWT Claims — Standard and Custom Claims Explained
direct_answer: JWT claims are key-value pairs in the token's payload that carry user identity and metadata. Standard registered claims include: sub (subject, usually user ID), iat (issued at timestamp), exp (expiration timestamp — always required for security), iss (issuer), aud (audience), and nbf (not before). Custom claims like roles or permissions can be added.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical JWT implementation knowledge — understanding claims shows you've actually built JWT auth, not just read about it
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Omitting the exp claim or not understanding that JWT has no built-in revocation — expiration is the only way to limit token lifetime
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish between registered claims (standardized), public claims (collision-resistant), and private claims (custom for your app), and explain security implications of each claim type

sections.title: Understanding JWT Claims and Their Types
sections.content:
Claims are the actual data stored in a JWT's payload — think of them as **key-value metadata** that describes the user and the token itself. There are three categories: **registered claims** are standardized by the JWT spec (like sub for user ID and exp for expiration) and recognized across systems, **public claims** are custom but registered in IANA JWT registry to avoid name collisions (like email or phone_number), and **private claims** are application-specific values you define yourself (like roles or tenant_id).

The most critical claim is **exp** (expiration) — without it, a stolen token works forever because JWT has no server-side revocation mechanism. Unlike sessions where you can invalidate a session ID in the database, JWTs are validated purely by signature, so expiration is your only defense against compromised tokens. Other essential claims: **sub** identifies the user (usually their database ID), **iat** records when the token was created (useful for security audits), and **iss** identifies who issued the token (important in multi-service environments to prevent token confusion attacks).

sections.title: Claim Types and Key Claims
sections.content:
blue|Registered|~spec-defined|sub = user ID, exp = expiry|iat = issued-at, iss = issuer|Understood by every JWT library
emerald|Public|~collision-safe|Registered in the IANA registry|Examples: email, phone_number|Avoids naming clashes across systems
violet|Private|~your app|Custom values you define|Examples: role, tenant_id|Keep the payload small
rose|exp is critical|~no revocation|JWT cannot be revoked server-side|Expiry is your only defense|Typically 15 minutes to 24 hours

sections.title: Building JWT with Standard and Custom Claims
When to Use Different Claim Types
sections.content:
Use **registered claims** (sub, exp, iat, iss, aud, nbf) in every production JWT — they're standardized and understood by all JWT libraries, making your tokens interoperable and following security best practices.

Use **private custom claims** for application-specific data like user roles, permissions, tenant IDs, or feature flags that your authorization logic needs — keep the payload under 1KB because tokens travel in every HTTP header.

Use the **aud** (audience) claim when one auth server issues tokens for multiple client apps, so services can reject tokens not intended for them, preventing token reuse attacks across services.

Use **nbf** (not before) claim when you issue tokens in advance but want them to become valid only at a future time, useful for scheduled access grants or time-based promotions.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting the exp claim**: Freshers create tokens without expiration thinking they'll handle it later, but this means stolen tokens work forever — always set exp to 15 minutes to 24 hours depending on security requirements.
- **Putting sensitive data in claims**: Since payload is base64-encoded (not encrypted), freshers store passwords, credit card numbers, or API secrets in custom claims where anyone who intercepts the token can read them.
- **Not validating aud and iss**: Freshers validate only the signature but ignore who issued the token or who it's for, allowing an attacker to reuse a legitimate token from one service against a different service if they share the same secret key.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **sub (subject)**: The user or entity the token represents — typically the user ID from your database, used for authorization decisions
**exp (expiration)**: Unix timestamp when token becomes invalid — ALWAYS required, typically 15 minutes to 24 hours from iat
**iat (issued at)**: Unix timestamp when token was created — useful for token age validation and security auditing
**iss (issuer)**: Identifies who created the token — prevents token confusion when multiple services issue tokens
**aud (audience)**: Identifies intended recipients — services should reject tokens where they're not in the audience list
**Custom claims**: Application-specific data like roles, permissions, tenant_id — keep payload small as it travels in every request header
**No revocation**: JWT has no built-in way to invalidate tokens server-side — expiration is the only defense, which is why short-lived tokens matter

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: JWT claims are the key-value pairs in the token's payload that carry information about the user and the token itself. There are three types. Registered claims are the standard ones defined in the JWT spec. The most important is exp for expiration — without it, a stolen token works forever because JWT doesn't have server-side revocation like sessions do. The sub claim is typically the user ID from your database. The iat claim records when the token was issued, which is useful for security audits. Then there's iss for issuer and aud for audience, which matter in multi-service environments to prevent token reuse attacks. The second type is public claims, which are custom but registered in a central registry to avoid naming conflicts across systems. The third type is private claims, which are application-specific values you define yourself. In a typical app, I'd add custom claims like role for authorization or tenant_id for multi-tenant apps. Here's the critical thing: always include the exp claim. Freshers sometimes skip it thinking they'll add it later, but that creates a massive security hole. If someone steals the token, it's valid forever until you rotate the global secret key, which invalidates every user's token. The other mistake is putting sensitive data in claims. The payload is base64-encoded, not encrypted. Anyone can decode it at jwt.io and read the claims. So never put passwords, API keys, or personally identifiable information you wouldn't want exposed. Keep claims minimal — just enough for authentication and authorization — because the entire token travels in the Authorization header on every request.

question: What library do you use to work with JWT in Spring Boot?
title: JWT Libraries in Spring Boot — JJWT and Spring Security OAuth2
direct_answer: The most popular library for JWT in Spring Boot is JJWT (Java JWT) by io.jsonwebtoken. It provides a fluent builder API for creating, parsing, and validating JWTs. You need three dependencies: jjwt-api, jjwt-impl, and jjwt-jackson. For OAuth2 or OpenID Connect flows, use spring-security-oauth2-resource-server, which has built-in JWT support with automatic validation and Spring Security integration.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical library knowledge and awareness of the JWT ecosystem in Java — shows you've implemented JWT, not just studied it theoretically
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing a library exists and trying to manually parse JWT with Base64 decoding and JSON parsing, which is error-prone and insecure
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention JJWT's version history (0.11+ uses new API), show awareness of the three required dependencies (api, impl, jackson), or mention spring-security-oauth2-resource-server for OAuth2 use cases

sections.title: JJWT: The Standard Java JWT Library
sections.content:
The go-to library for JWT in Spring Boot is **JJWT** (io.jsonwebtoken), which provides a clean, type-safe API for creating, signing, parsing, and validating JSON Web Tokens. JJWT handles the cryptographic heavy lifting: signing tokens with HMAC or RSA keys, verifying signatures, checking expiration, and parsing claims.

You need **three Maven dependencies**: jjwt-api (the interface), jjwt-impl (the implementation), and jjwt-jackson (JSON serialization). The library follows a builder pattern that makes token creation readable and less error-prone. For **OAuth2 or OpenID Connect** scenarios (like integrating with Keycloak, Auth0, or Google login), Spring Security provides **spring-security-oauth2-resource-server**, which includes JWT support out of the box and integrates tightly with Spring Security's filter chain. This is the production-grade choice when you're consuming JWTs from an external identity provider rather than generating your own.

sections.title: Which JWT Library?
sections.content:
blue|JJWT|~io.jsonwebtoken|Fluent builder + parser API|You issue your own tokens|Needs jjwt-api, jjwt-impl, jjwt-jackson
emerald|OAuth2 Resource Server|~spring-security|Validates tokens from a provider|Fetches keys from a JWKS endpoint|For Keycloak, Auth0, Okta, Google
amber|Decision rule|~issue vs validate|Issuing tokens yourself -> JJWT|Validating external tokens -> Resource Server|Never hand-parse JWT with Base64

sections.title: Creating and Validating JWT with JJWT
When to Use Each Library
sections.content: **Use JJWT** when you're building custom authentication in your Spring Boot app and need to generate your own JWTs. This is typical for internal REST APIs, mobile app backends, or microservices where you control the entire auth flow from login to token issuance. JJWT gives you full control over claims, signing algorithms, and expiration. **Use spring-security-oauth2-resource-server** when you're integrating with an external identity provider like Keycloak, Okta, Auth0, or Google. Your app becomes a resource server that validates JWTs issued by the provider. Spring Security handles the heavy lifting: fetching public keys from the provider's JWKS endpoint, validating signatures, checking expiration, and mapping claims to Spring Security authorities. You configure it with application.yml properties and it just works. If you're unsure, ask: am I issuing tokens or just validating them? Issuing = JJWT. Validating from external provider = OAuth2 resource server.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using only jjwt-api dependency**: Freshers add just the API jar and get NoClassDefFoundError at runtime because the implementation (jjwt-impl) and JSON parser (jjwt-jackson) are missing. All three dependencies are required.
- **Manually parsing JWT with Base64**: Trying to decode the token by splitting on dots and Base64-decoding each part, then using Jackson to parse JSON. This skips signature validation entirely — a massive security hole. Always use a library.
- **Hardcoding secrets in code**: Storing the signing key as a string literal in the service class. Keys should come from environment variables or a secrets manager, never committed to Git.
- **Not understanding JJWT 0.11+ breaking changes**: Older tutorials use deprecated APIs like signWith(SignatureAlgorithm, key). The modern API uses signWith(key) and type-safe builders.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **JJWT (io.jsonwebtoken)**: The standard Java library for creating, signing, parsing, and validating JWTs
**Three dependencies**: jjwt-api (interfaces), jjwt-impl (implementation), jjwt-jackson (JSON serialization)
**Fluent API**: Builder pattern for token creation and parser for validation with automatic signature checking
**spring-security-oauth2-resource-server**: Spring's built-in JWT support for OAuth2/OIDC integration
**Use JJWT when**: You generate your own tokens in a custom auth flow
**Use OAuth2 resource server when**: You validate tokens from external providers (Keycloak, Auth0, Google)
**Security**: Never manually parse JWT with Base64 — libraries handle signature validation correctly

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The most popular library is JJWT, which stands for Java JWT, from the io.jsonwebtoken group. It gives you a fluent builder API for creating and validating tokens. You need three Maven dependencies: jjwt-api for the interfaces, jjwt-impl for the actual implementation, and jjwt-jackson for JSON serialization. The library handles all the cryptographic details like signing with HMAC or RSA, verifying signatures, and checking expiration. You build a token by calling Jwts.builder, setting the subject and claims, adding an expiration date, and signing it with a secret key. To validate, you use Jwts.parser with the same key, and it automatically checks the signature and expiry. If you're working with OAuth2 or OpenID Connect, like integrating with Keycloak or Google login, you'd use spring-security-oauth2-resource-server instead. That's Spring Security's built-in JWT support for validating tokens from external identity providers. It fetches public keys from the provider's JWKS endpoint and handles everything through configuration. The key is: use JJWT when you're issuing your own tokens, use OAuth2 resource server when you're validating tokens from someone else.

seo.metaDescription: Learn JJWT library for JWT in Spring Boot — builder API, parsing, ExpiredJwtException, SignatureException, and Spring Security OAuth2 JWT alternative.

speakable_v2.hook: You can theoretically parse a JWT manually with Base64 decoding, but no one does that in practice — JJWT gives you a clean API that handles signing, parsing, and validation in a few lines.

beats.content: JJWT — io.jsonwebtoken — is the standard JWT library for Java and Spring Boot projects. You add the jjwt-api, jjwt-impl, and jjwt-jackson dependencies and you're ready to generate and validate tokens.

For generating, you use Jwts.builder(), chain methods to set the subject, add custom claims, set the issued-at and expiration times, call signWith() with your SecretKey, and compact() to get the final token string.

For parsing, you use Jwts.parser(), provide the secret key for signature verification, build it, then call parseSignedClaims() with the token. You get back a Claims object where you can read the subject, expiration, and any custom claims.

non-obvious: JJWT throws specific exceptions you must handle in your JWT filter. ExpiredJwtException means the token is past its exp time — return 401. SignatureException means the token was tampered with or signed with a different key — also return 401. Letting these propagate as 500 errors is a common mistake.

speakable_v2.cap: JJWT is the standard choice. Builder to generate, parser to validate, catch ExpiredJwtException and SignatureException in your filter and return clean 401 responses.
followup_handoff: Generating a proper SecretKey — Keys.hmacShaKeyFor from a base64-encoded secret — is worth knowing for interviews.
Spring Security OAuth2 Resource Server is the alternative for OAuth2 and JWKS-based JWT validation at scale.

question: How does JWT-based authentication work in Spring Boot?
title: JWT Authentication Flow in Spring Boot — Request Lifecycle
direct_answer: JWT-based authentication in Spring Boot follows this flow: User logs in with credentials, server validates them and generates a signed JWT containing user info and expiration. Client stores the JWT and sends it in the Authorization: Bearer header with each request. A custom Spring Security filter intercepts requests, extracts and validates the JWT signature and expiry, then populates the SecurityContext with user details so Spring Security can authorize the request.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of end-to-end JWT authentication flow and how it integrates with Spring Security's filter chain
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing how the JWT gets from client to server (Authorization header) or how Spring Security's SecurityContext gets populated from the token
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Walk through the complete flow including filter chain order, mention OncePerRequestFilter, and explain why JWT enables stateless auth

sections.title: JWT Authentication Flow in Spring Boot
sections.content:
Spring Boot JWT authentication replaces traditional session-based auth with a **token-based stateless model**. The flow starts when a user POSTs credentials to a /login endpoint — your authentication service validates the username and password against the database, then generates a JWT containing the user's ID and roles using a library like jjwt.

The client receives this token and stores it (usually in localStorage or a cookie). On subsequent requests, the client includes the token in the **Authorization header** with the format Bearer eyJhbGc.... Here's where Spring Security's filter chain comes in: you create a custom filter (extending OncePerRequestFilter) that runs before Spring's authentication filters. This custom filter extracts the token from the header, validates the signature using your secret key, checks the expiration timestamp, and if valid, creates an **Authentication object** with the user's details and sets it in Spring's SecurityContext. From that point on, Spring Security's authorization mechanisms (like at-PreAuthorize annotations) work normally because the SecurityContext has the authenticated user. The beauty: no server-side session storage needed.

sections.title: JWT Login and Request Flows
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TD A[POST /login
username + password] --> B[Validate credentials] B --> C[Generate signed JWT] C --> D[Return token to client] D --> E[Client stores token] E --> F[Each request:
Authorization: Bearer token] F --> G[JwtAuthenticationFilter
OncePerRequestFilter] G --> H{Signature + expiry valid?} H -->|Yes| I[Set Authentication
in SecurityContext] H -->|No| J[401 Unauthorized] I --> K[Controller runs] ```

sections.title: JWT Authentication Filter Implementation
When to Use JWT Authentication
sections.content: Use JWT in **REST APIs** consumed by mobile apps or SPAs where you need stateless authentication — each request is independent and the server doesn't maintain session state. Perfect for **microservices architectures** where multiple services need to verify user identity without querying a central session database — services can validate tokens using a shared secret or public key. Ideal for **horizontally scaled applications** behind a load balancer where sessions would require sticky sessions or distributed session storage — JWT eliminates that complexity. Also use JWT when building **public APIs** where third-party clients authenticate with API keys but you still need user-level authorization — the JWT can carry both API client identity and end-user claims in a single token.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not adding the filter to the chain**: Freshers create a JwtAuthenticationFilter but forget to register it in SecurityFilterChain configuration before UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter, so the filter never runs and requests stay unauthenticated.
- **Populating SecurityContext after authentication**: Setting the Authentication object in SecurityContext when the user is already authenticated causes Spring to re-authenticate on every request, defeating stateless benefits — check if authentication is null first.
- **Missing token expiration checks**: Validating only the signature but not checking the exp claim means expired tokens still work, creating a security hole where stolen tokens never become invalid.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Login flow**: POST credentials to /login endpoint, server validates against database, generates JWT with user claims, returns token to client
**Authorization header**: Client sends token in every request as Authorization: Bearer <token> — this is the standard way to transmit tokens
**Custom filter**: Extend OncePerRequestFilter and register it before Spring's authentication filters to intercept and validate tokens
**Token extraction**: Parse Authorization header, remove Bearer prefix, validate signature and expiration using jjwt or similar library
**SecurityContext population**: Create UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken with user details and set it in SecurityContextHolder for request scope
**Filter chain order**: Your JWT filter must run before UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter so Spring doesn't try session-based auth first
**Stateless benefit**: No server-side session storage needed — all user info travels with the token, enabling easy horizontal scaling

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: JWT authentication in Spring Boot starts when a user logs in by sending their username and password to a login endpoint. The server validates those credentials against the database, and if they're correct, it generates a JWT token containing the user's ID and roles, plus an expiration timestamp. The server sends this token back to the client. From that point on, the client includes the token in the Authorization header of every request using the format Bearer followed by the token. Now here's where Spring Security comes in. You create a custom filter that extends OncePerRequestFilter, and you register it in the SecurityFilterChain before the standard authentication filters. This filter runs on every request. It extracts the token from the Authorization header, validates the signature to make sure no one tampered with it, and checks that it hasn't expired. If the token is valid, the filter creates an Authentication object containing the user's details and sets it in Spring's SecurityContext. That's crucial because once the SecurityContext has the authentication, all of Spring Security's authorization mechanisms work normally — like PreAuthorize annotations on your controller methods. The request continues through the filter chain, hits your controller, and Spring knows who the user is. One thing freshers miss is the filter chain order. If you don't register your JWT filter before UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter, Spring tries session-based auth first and your JWT logic never runs. The beauty of this approach is it's completely stateless — the server doesn't store any session data, so you can scale horizontally without worrying about sticky sessions or distributed caches.

seo.metaTitle: JWT Authentication Flow in Spring Boot | Java Fresher Interview
seo.metaDescription: Learn JWT authentication flow in Spring Boot — login endpoint, token generation, JwtAuthenticationFilter, SecurityContext population, stateless sessions.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API with JWT-based authentication
speakable_v2.hook: JWT authentication is two completely separate flows — a login flow that runs once, and a validation flow that runs on every single request. Knowing both in detail is essential.

beats.content: The login flow: the client POSTs credentials to /api/auth/login. Your controller calls AuthenticationManager.authenticate() to verify them. If successful, a JwtService generates a signed token with the user's ID and roles and returns it to the client. The server stores nothing.

The request flow: on every subsequent request, the client puts the JWT in the Authorization header as a Bearer token. A custom filter — extending OncePerRequestFilter — intercepts the request, extracts the token, validates the signature and expiry via JwtService, loads the user's UserDetails, and sets an authenticated token in the SecurityContext.

You register this custom filter in SecurityConfig with addFilterBefore, positioning it before UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter. Session policy is set to STATELESS so Spring never creates a server-side session — the SecurityContext is rebuilt from the JWT on every request.

candidates miss: the SecurityContext does NOT persist between requests in stateless mode. The JWT filter must set it on every single request, or the request will be treated as unauthenticated even if a valid token was sent.

speakable_v2.cap: Login once to get a token, then send the token on every request. The server validates the signature and rebuilds context each time — no sessions, no shared state, scales to any number of servers.
followup_handoff: Implementing the JwtAuthenticationFilter with OncePerRequestFilter is a common practical follow-up.
Token expiry handling — specifically ExpiredJwtException and refresh token rotation — is the natural next topic.

question: Where should you store JWT tokens on the client side?
title: JWT Storage — localStorage vs HttpOnly Cookie Security Trade-offs
direct_answer: The two main options are localStorage and HttpOnly cookies, each with different security trade-offs. localStorage is accessible by JavaScript, making it vulnerable to XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) attacks where malicious scripts steal the token. HttpOnly cookies are not accessible by JavaScript, preventing XSS theft, but are vulnerable to CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) attacks, which can be mitigated with SameSite=Strict.

interviewer_intent.testing: Security awareness and understanding of client-side attack vectors — essential for any full-stack or backend role dealing with authentication
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Recommending localStorage without mentioning XSS risks, or not understanding the CSRF vs XSS trade-off between the two storage options
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Demonstrate knowledge of both XSS and CSRF attack vectors, explain the role of SameSite attribute, and mention Content Security Policy as an additional defense layer

sections.title: Client-Side JWT Storage Options and Security Trade-offs
sections.content:
Storing JWT tokens on the client is a critical security decision that involves choosing between two attack surfaces. **localStorage** is the simplest approach — the token lives in the browser's storage API and JavaScript can read it to add to request headers. The risk: any JavaScript code on the page can access it, so if an attacker injects malicious JavaScript through an XSS vulnerability (like a comment section that doesn't sanitize HTML), they can steal the token. **HttpOnly cookies** are set by the server with the HttpOnly flag, which prevents JavaScript from accessing them — the browser automatically includes them in requests to the same domain.

This blocks XSS token theft, but opens CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) attacks where a malicious site tricks the browser into making authenticated requests to your API. The defense: the **SameSite** cookie attribute. SameSite=Strict prevents the browser from sending the cookie on cross-site requests, eliminating CSRF risk. The choice depends on your architecture: SPAs often use localStorage with strong Content Security Policy headers, while server-rendered apps prefer HttpOnly cookies with SameSite=Strict.

sections.title: Two Storage Options, Two Risks
sections.content:
rose|localStorage|~JS-accessible|Easy to read/write from JavaScript|Vulnerable to XSS token theft|Mitigate with a strong CSP header
emerald|HttpOnly cookie|~JS cannot read|Browser sends it automatically|Blocks XSS theft of the token|Vulnerable to CSRF — use SameSite=Strict
blue|Best practice|~production|HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite=Strict|Short-lived access token|Refresh token for renewal

rows: High — any JavaScript can read token
Manual — add Authorization header in code
Works — send token to any domain

sections.title: Storing in localStorage (XSS-exposed)
Storing in an HttpOnly Cookie (XSS-safe)
Choosing the Right Storage Strategy
sections.content:
Use **localStorage** for single-page applications (SPAs) that communicate with a separate API domain, especially when building mobile apps alongside the web app — both can use the same token-based authentication. Add a strong Content Security Policy (CSP) header to block inline scripts and restrict script sources, dramatically reducing XSS risk.

Use **HttpOnly cookies with SameSite=Strict** for server-rendered applications where the frontend and API are on the same domain — the browser handles security automatically and CSRF is prevented.

Use **HttpOnly cookies with SameSite=Lax** if you need to support legitimate cross-site navigation (like OAuth redirects or email links) but still want CSRF protection for state-changing requests. For maximum security in high-stakes applications, use **short-lived access tokens in memory** (lost on page refresh) with longer-lived refresh tokens in HttpOnly cookies, combining the XSS protection of cookies with limited attack window.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using localStorage without CSP**: Freshers store tokens in localStorage for convenience but don't implement Content Security Policy headers, leaving the app wide open to XSS attacks where any injected script can steal tokens and impersonate users.
- **Setting regular cookies instead of HttpOnly**: Creating cookies with document.cookie means JavaScript can still read them, defeating the entire purpose — the server must set the HttpOnly flag in the Set-Cookie response header.
- **Ignoring SameSite attribute**: Setting HttpOnly cookies without SameSite=Strict or Lax leaves the app vulnerable to CSRF where attackers trick users into making authenticated requests to your API from malicious sites.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)**: Attack where malicious JavaScript executes on your page — can steal tokens from localStorage but not HttpOnly cookies
**CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery)**: Attack where malicious site makes authenticated requests using your cookies — prevented by SameSite attribute
**HttpOnly flag**: Server-side cookie attribute that prevents JavaScript access — set in Set-Cookie header, not accessible via document.cookie
**SameSite=Strict**: Cookie only sent on same-site requests — strongest CSRF protection but breaks legitimate cross-site navigation
**SameSite=Lax**: Cookie sent on same-site requests and top-level GET navigations — balances security with usability for links and redirects
**Content Security Policy (CSP)**: HTTP header that restricts script sources — mitigates XSS risk when using localStorage by blocking inline and untrusted scripts
**Token rotation**: Store short-lived access tokens (15 min) with long-lived refresh tokens (7 days) in HttpOnly cookies — limits damage window if stolen

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The two main options for storing JWT tokens on the client are localStorage and HttpOnly cookies, and they have opposite security trade-offs. If you use localStorage, your JavaScript code can read the token and add it to the Authorization header manually. That's convenient and works great for SPAs and mobile apps. The problem is XSS attacks. If an attacker finds any way to inject JavaScript into your page — maybe through a comment field that doesn't sanitize HTML — they can steal the token from localStorage and send it to their server. Once they have it, they can impersonate the user. Now, HttpOnly cookies are different. The server sets them with a special HttpOnly flag, and JavaScript can't access them at all. The browser automatically includes them in requests to your domain. This blocks XSS theft completely. But it opens a different attack called CSRF. A malicious site can trick the user's browser into making authenticated requests to your API because the browser auto-sends the cookie. The defense is the SameSite attribute. If you set SameSite equals Strict, the browser won't send the cookie on requests from other sites, which kills CSRF. So here's how I'd decide. For a single-page app that talks to a separate API domain, I'd use localStorage but add a strong Content Security Policy header to block inline scripts and restrict where scripts can load from. That dramatically reduces XSS risk. For a server-rendered app where the frontend and backend are on the same domain, I'd use HttpOnly cookies with SameSite equals Strict because the browser handles everything automatically and CSRF is prevented. One mistake freshers make is using localStorage without CSP, leaving the door wide open for XSS. Another is setting regular cookies with JavaScript instead of having the server set HttpOnly cookies, which defeats the whole purpose.

speakable_v2.hook: Where you store a JWT on the client is a security decision — both options have a serious attack vector, and knowing the trade-off is what interviewers are actually testing.

beats.content: localStorage is the simple option. Your JavaScript code can read and write to it easily, and you attach the token manually to the Authorization header on each request. The problem is XSS — if an attacker manages to inject malicious JavaScript into your page, it can call localStorage.getItem and steal the token instantly.

HttpOnly cookies solve XSS because the HttpOnly flag prevents JavaScript from accessing the cookie at all — only the browser sends it. The new problem is CSRF — a malicious site can trigger requests to your API and the browser will automatically include the cookie. You mitigate this with the SameSite=Strict attribute, which tells the browser not to send the cookie on cross-origin requests.

production trap: many tutorials default to localStorage for simplicity. In production with real user data, HttpOnly cookie with Secure and SameSite=Strict is the safer choice — it eliminates the XSS token theft risk entirely.

speakable_v2.cap: No storage option is risk-free. HttpOnly cookie plus SameSite=Strict is generally the stronger choice for production because it prevents XSS-based token theft.
followup_handoff: Content Security Policy is a browser-level defense that reduces XSS risk when using localStorage.
We can also look at in-memory token storage — the most secure option but impractical for most apps because the token is lost on page refresh.

question: What is the difference between stateful and stateless authentication?
title: Stateful vs Stateless Authentication — Session vs JWT
direct_answer: Stateful authentication stores session data on the server (in memory, Redis, or a database) and gives the client a session ID cookie. The server looks up session data on every request. Stateless authentication (JWT) embeds all user information inside the token itself. The server validates the token's signature and expiry without storing anything. Stateless enables horizontal scaling without shared session storage, but you cannot revoke tokens before they expire.

interviewer_intent.testing: Architectural understanding of authentication approaches and how they impact system scalability and session management
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying JWT is always better without acknowledging the revocation problem — tokens can't be invalidated before expiration in pure stateless systems
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the horizontal scaling benefit clearly, mention the session storage challenge (sticky sessions or Redis), and describe real-world hybrid approaches (short-lived JWT + refresh token blacklist)

sections.title: Two Fundamentally Different Approaches to Authentication
sections.content:
The core difference is **where user session data lives**. In **stateful authentication**, the server maintains session state in memory, a database, or Redis.

After login, the server creates a session object containing user details, permissions, and metadata, then sends a session ID cookie to the client. On each request, the client sends this cookie, and the server looks up the full session. In **stateless authentication** (typically JWT), the server creates a cryptographically signed token containing all necessary user information (user ID, roles, expiration). The client sends this token in the Authorization header on each request. The server validates the signature and reads the data directly from the token without any database lookup. Think of stateful like a coat check: you get a ticket (session ID) and the server keeps your coat (session data). Stateless is like wearing your coat everywhere: all your information travels with you (the token).

sections.title: Where the State Lives
sections.content:
blue|Stateful (Sessions)|~server remembers|Session stored in memory/Redis/DB|Client holds only a session ID cookie|Instant revocation by deleting the session
emerald|Stateless (JWT)|~token remembers|All claims live inside the signed token|Server stores nothing|Scales horizontally with no shared store
amber|Hybrid|~best of both|Short-lived access JWT (15 min)|Refresh token stored server-side|Scaling plus a revocation escape hatch

rows: Requires sticky sessions or shared Redis

sections.title: Stateful Session Configuration
Stateless JWT Configuration
When to Choose Each Approach
sections.content: **Use stateful sessions** when you need immediate revocation control (admin panels, banking apps where you must terminate sessions instantly), when your infrastructure already has Redis or a session store, or when you have long-lived sessions with frequently changing permissions (the server can update session data without issuing new tokens). **Use stateless JWT** when you're building microservices that need to scale horizontally without shared state, when you have mobile apps or SPAs that prefer token-based auth, or when you need cross-domain authentication (JWT works across different subdomains easily). Real-world systems often use **hybrid approaches**: short-lived access tokens (JWT, 15 minutes) for stateless requests, plus a refresh token stored server-side with revocation capability. This gives you scaling benefits with an escape hatch for security.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Claiming JWT is always better**: Freshers see "stateless" and "scalable" and assume JWT is the modern choice for everything, ignoring that you lose instant revocation. If a JWT is stolen, it's valid until expiry — you can't kill it.
- **Not understanding the scaling trade-off**: Saying stateful doesn't scale misses the point. Stateful requires sticky sessions (routing the same user to the same server) or a shared session store like Redis. Both work at scale, but add complexity.
- **Storing too much in JWT**: Putting the entire user profile in a token bloats every request. JWT should contain only identity claims (user ID, roles) — fetch other data from the database when needed.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Stateful**: Server stores session data, client sends session ID cookie, server looks up data on each request
**Stateless**: All user info in signed token, server validates signature and reads claims without storage
**Scaling**: Stateful needs sticky sessions or Redis; stateless scales horizontally without shared state
**Revocation**: Stateful allows instant session deletion; stateless cannot revoke tokens before expiry
**Hybrid approach**: Short-lived JWT (15 min) + refresh token with server-side blacklist balances both
**Token size**: JWT travels in every request header, larger than a session ID cookie
**Security model**: Stateful keeps control server-side; stateless delegates trust to signature verification

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The key difference is where session data lives. In stateful authentication, the server stores session information in memory, a database, or Redis. When you log in, the server creates a session object with your user ID, roles, and other details, then gives you a session ID in a cookie. On every request, the server looks up your session using that ID. In stateless authentication, usually with JWT, the server doesn't store anything. Instead, it creates a signed token containing all your user information. You send this token in the Authorization header with each request, and the server just validates the signature and reads the claims from the token itself. The big advantage of stateless is horizontal scaling. You don't need sticky sessions or a shared Redis instance because any server can validate the token. But there's a trade-off: you can't revoke a JWT before it expires. If someone steals the token, it's valid until expiry. With stateful sessions, you can delete the session from storage immediately. In production, many systems use a hybrid approach: short-lived access tokens, maybe fifteen minutes, combined with a refresh token that's stored server-side so you can revoke it if needed. This gives you the scaling benefits of stateless with an escape hatch for security.

seo.metaTitle: Stateful vs Stateless Authentication — Session vs JWT | Interview
seo.metaDescription: Learn stateful vs stateless authentication — server-side sessions vs JWT, horizontal scaling advantage, JWT invalidation problem, Spring Security STATELESS.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API with JWT-based authentication
speakable_v2.hook: Stateful and stateless authentication have a fundamental trade-off — and explaining the scaling advantage of JWT without knowing its revocation limitation tells an interviewer you only know half the picture.

beats.content: Stateful authentication stores session data on the server. When you log in, the server creates a session entry in memory or a database. Every request carries a session ID cookie, and the server looks up that ID to identify you. Session invalidation is instant — just delete the session record.

The scaling problem: with multiple servers, Server B doesn't have Server A's sessions. You need sticky sessions — routing every user to the same server — or a shared session store like Redis. Both add complexity and cost.

JWT is stateless — the server stores nothing after issuing the token. Any server can validate any JWT independently by checking the signature. That's why JWT is the standard for microservices and horizontally scaled systems.

gotcha: JWT's statelessness is also its weakness. You can't revoke a JWT before it expires. If a token is stolen, the attacker has valid access until expiry. Solutions are keeping expiry short — 15 minutes — and using refresh tokens, or maintaining a Redis blacklist of revoked tokens.

speakable_v2.cap: Sessions scale badly but revoke instantly. JWT scales perfectly but can't be revoked before expiry. Short expiry plus refresh tokens is the practical middle ground.
followup_handoff: Refresh token rotation is how most production systems handle the JWT revocation problem.
Spring Security's SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS is how you tell Spring not to create sessions for JWT-based APIs.
